Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verse 1–2:

(p-176) Sūrat al-Raḥmān

Makkiyya (Meccan) or Madaniyya (Medinan) or mutabaʿḍiḍa (partly Meccan, partly Medinan), and its verses are seventy-eight.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

When, in the preceding surah, he enumerated what befell the earlier nations of the various kinds of Allah's, mighty and majestic is He, retribution, and after each kind he explained that the Qur'an had been made easy for the purpose of bringing people to remembrance and admonition, and he reproached them for their turning away from that, he enumerated in this noble surah the diverse kinds of His blessings—religious, worldly, personal and cosmic—that He has poured out upon all of mankind, and after each category of them he rebuked them for their failure to fulfil the obligations of gratitude for them. ﴿The Most Gracious﴾ ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾

﴿The Most Gracious﴾ ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ because it is the greatest of blessings in importance and the loftiest in station. How could it not be? There is no goal toward which the eyes of nations gaze except that it is its source and its focus, and no aim toward which the necks of aspirations stretch except that it is its path and its way. The attribution of its teaching to the name al-Raḥmān is to signal that it is among the effects of the all-encompassing mercy and its judgments. Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verses 3–4:

﴿He created man﴾ ﴿taught him al-bayan (clear expression)﴾. This is to specify the one taught (the human being) and to clarify the manner of the teaching. What is meant by the creation of man is bringing him into being in the state in which he is, with his outward and inward faculties. Al-bayan is the expression of what is in the heart (damir). The intended meaning of his being taught is not merely enabling man to express himself, but also, from that, enabling him to understand the expression of others, since it is upon this that the teaching of the Qur'an depends. The three clauses are consecutive predicates (akhbar mutaradifah) of al-Rahman, and the omission of the conjunction (al-'atif) from the last two is because they come in the manner of enumeration (al-ta'did).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verses 3–4:

The three clauses are consecutive predicates (akhbar mutaradifah) of al-Rahman, and the omission of the conjunction (al-'atif) from the last two is because they come in the manner of enumeration (al-ta'did).

The sun and the moon [run] by a precise reckoning.

﴿The sun and the moon [run] by a precise reckoning﴾ means: they move by a fixed calculation in their zodiacal stations (burūj) and their mansions (manāzil), by which the affairs of the lower world (al-kā'inat al-sufliyyah) are ordered, the seasons and times vary, and the years and the reckoning (al-ḥisāb) are known.

(p-177) ﴿And the star﴾, i.e., the plant that comes up (yanjum, i.e., rises) out of the earth and has no stem.

﴿And the tree﴾, i.e., that which has a stem.

﴿Both prostrate﴾, i.e., they submit to Him, the Exalted, in what He wills for them by nature, submitting as prostrating ones among the responsible (mukallafin) submit willingly. The two clauses are two further predicates of "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman), stripped of a verbal connective, relying on the complete strength of the semantic connection, since it is not imagined that the mind would turn to the sun and moon being subjected by other than Him, nor to the prostration of the star and tree being directed to anything other than Him. It is as if it were said: "The sun and the moon are by reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate to Him." The omission of the conjunction from the first clause, for the reason mentioned earlier, and the insertion of the conjunction between it and the second, is for their correspondence in terms of contrast, since the sun and moon are celestial (ulwiyyan) and the star and tree are terrestrial (sufliyyan), and because the state of each of the celestial pair and the state of the terrestrial pair belong to the category of submission to the command of God, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verse 7:

﴿And the heaven He raised high﴾. That is: He created it elevated in station and rank, inasmuch as He made it the source of His decrees and judgments, the place where His commands descend, and the abode of His angels. In this there is an indication of the magnificence of His majesty and the greatness of His dominion and sovereignty, which is not hidden. It has also been read as "wa-al-samā'u rafa'ahā" with the raising (rafʿ) [of al-samā'], on the basis of it being the subject of the sentence (al-ibtidā').

﴿And He set up the balance﴾. That is: He legislated justice (al-ʿadl) and commanded it, by granting every entitled party what it deserved and giving every possessor of a right his right, so that by it the affair of the world is put in order and kept upright. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By justice the heavens and the earth stand." It has been said: on this view, "the balance" (al-mīzān) is the Qur'an, and this is the view of al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the balance﴾. It has also been said: it is that by which the measures of things are known, such as the scale, the measuring vessel and the like, and this is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Dahhak. The meaning then is: He created it placed low upon the earth, inasmuch as He attached to it the judgments of His servants and their affairs, and what He obligated them to in terms of equality and fairness in taking from them and giving to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verse 8:

﴿That you not transgress in the balance﴾ That is: so that you do not transgress in it. Here "an" (أنْ) is a subjunctive particle (nasiba) and "la" (لا) is a negation particle, and a lam of causation (lam al-'illa) is assumed (muqaddara), attached to His words, exalted is He: ﴿And He set up the balance﴾. Or: "that you do not transgress" is explanatory (mufassira), for what the sense of saying (al-qawl) implies in the law (al-shar'), and "la" is a prohibitive particle (nahiya), meaning: do not overstep, and do not go beyond equity (al-insaf). It has also been read "la tatghaw" (لا تَطْغَوْا) with the implied sense of saying (irada al-qawl).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verse 9:

﴿And establish the weight with justice﴾ — make your weighing upright by means of justice. It has also been said: establish the tongue of the balance (lisan al-mizan, the pointer) with justice and equity. It has also been said: the establishing is by the hand and the justice is by the heart.

﴿And do not make the balance deficient﴾ — that is, do not diminish it. He first commanded equalization, then forbade transgression (tughyan), which is aggression and excess, then forbade deficiency (khusran), which is cheating (tatfif) and shortfall. He repeated the word "mizan" to emphasize the injunction concerning it and to stress the command to use it and to urge it. It has also been read as "wa la takhsaruu" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma or kasra on the sin, and it is said: khasira al-mizan yakhsaru and yakhsiruhu. It is also read with a fatha on the sin, on the basis that the original is "wa la takhsaru" (p-178) "fi al-mizan," so the preposition was deleted and the verb was made to reach its object directly.

And the earth He has laid down for all creatures (﴿والأرْضَ وضَعَها﴾): that is, He lowered it, spread out upon the water.

﴿لِلأنامِ﴾: that is, for the creation. It has been said that what is meant by it is every living being; it has been said that it is every creature upon the surface of the earth; and it has been said that it is the two weighty ones (humans and jinn).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verse 11:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Therein is fruit﴾ ... etc. It is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought in to confirm what the preceding sentence conveyed, namely that the earth was laid out for the benefit of mankind (al-anam), and to detail the benefits that return to human beings. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) referring to "the earth." In that case, the better reading is that the circumstantial element is the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur), and "fruit" (fakihah) is in the nominative as the agent (al-fa'iliyyah), meaning: therein are many kinds of things by which one takes delight and enjoyment (yatafakkahu bihi).

﴿And the palm tree, with its sheaths﴾: al-akmam are the containers of the fruit, plural of kumm, or everything that covers (yukamm), i.e., is wrapped in fiber, palm fronds, and the spathe (kafrra). These too are among the things from which benefit is derived, like the fruit, the heart of the palm (jummar), and the trunks that are enclosed within them.

﴿And the grain﴾ is that which is eaten as food, such as wheat and barley.

﴿Possessing the husk﴾ is the leafage of the crop. It is also said to be the chaff.

﴿And the fragrant plant﴾. It is said to be sustenance, and by it is meant the kernel, that is: in them is what is enjoyed of fruits. What combines enjoyment and nourishment is the fruit of the palm and what is eaten. The grain that has a husk is the fodder of livestock, and the fragrant plant is the food of people. It is also read as "and the grain, possessing the husk, and the fragrant plant," meaning: He created the grain and the fragrant plant, or I single them out. It is permissible that what is meant is "and the possessor of the fragrant plant," so the governing noun (al-mudaf) is omitted and the governed noun (al-mudaf ilayh) is put in its place. As for "al-Rayhan," it is either fa'ilan from rawh, so the waw is changed to ya' and assimilated (idgham), then lightened (takhfif); or fa'lan, whose waw is changed to ya' for lightening, or to distinguish it from al-Rawhan, which is that which has spirit. This is what al-Qurtubi said.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verse 13:

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ The address is to the two weighty things (al-thaqalan, humans and jinn), indicated by His words, exalted is He, ﴿for all creatures﴾, and His words, exalted is He, ﴿We will soon attend to you, O two weighty ones﴾ will make it explicit. The fa' (then) denotes the sequence of denunciation and rebuke upon what has been detailed of the varieties of bounties and the kinds of favours that necessitate faith and gratitude. The mention of the title "Lord" (rububiyyah), which points to absolute ownership and nurturing, together with its attribution to their pronoun, serves to emphasise the censure and intensify the rebuke. As for the meaning of their denying His favours, exalted is He, it is their disbelief in them, either by denying that it is a favour in itself, such as the teaching of the Qur'an and the religious blessings that rest upon it, or by denying that it comes from God, exalted is He, while acknowledging that it is a favour in itself, such as the worldly blessings reaching them, by attributing it to other than God, exalted is He, either independently or by association, explicitly or implicitly. For their associating their gods with Him, exalted is He, in worship is among the motives for their associating them with Him in what necessitates it. The expression of their aforementioned disbelief as denial is because the indication of the mentioned favours on the obligation of faith and gratitude is a testimony from them to that; so their disbelief in them is necessarily a denial of them. That is: when the matter is as has been detailed, then which of the individual favours of your Owner and Nurturer will you both deny? Yet each of them speaks the truth and bears witness to sincerity.

(p-179) ﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾ — a preface to the reproach for their failure to fulfill the duties of gratitude for the blessing that pertains to the very essence of each of the two weighty creations (jinn and humankind). "Ṣalṣāl" (ṣalṣāl): dry clay that gives forth a ringing sound. "Fakhkhār" (fakhkhār): earthenware. God Most High created Adam, peace be upon him, from dust which He made into clay, then into black mud molded into shape (ḥama' masnūn), then into ṣalṣāl; so there is no contradiction between the verse that speaks of one of these stages and what speaks of another of the two.

**Qur'an 55:15:** ﴿And He created the jinn﴾. That is: the jinn, or the father of the jinn.

﴿from smokeless fire﴾. That is: from pure flame of fire.

﴿of fire﴾. This is an explanation (bayan) of "marij," for it originally refers to that which is agitated, from *maraja*, meaning it became agitated.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verses 16–17:

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ — that is, of the abundant blessings He bestowed upon you both within the make-up of your creation.

﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ — read in the nominative (marfu') as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: "He who did the wondrous deeds mentioned is the Lord of the two risings of summer and winter and their two settings." And from His authority it follows that He is the Lord of everything that exists between them, entirely. It was also said: it is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is His words, exalted is He, ﴿He let loose﴾ ... etc. It has also been read in the genitive (jarr), as a substitute (badal) for "your Lord."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verses 18–19:

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ Among what is in that are countless benefits: the moderation of the air, the alternation of the seasons, and the occurrence, at its time, of what suits each season, and so on.

﴿He released the two seas, meeting each other.﴾

﴿He released the two seas﴾ means: He let them loose, from "maraja al-dabbah" (he let the animal go free), when I let the animal go. The meaning is: He released the salty sea and the sweet sea.

﴿Meeting each other﴾ means: they are adjacent, and their surfaces touch with no separation between them to the eye. It is also said: He released the two seas of Persia and Rome, meeting each other in the Ocean, because they are two gulfs branching off from it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verses 21–22:

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ And there is nothing of them that could accept denial.

﴿From them come forth the pearl and the coral.﴾ (p-180) "Al-lu'lu'" (pearl) is al-durr (the pearl), and "al-marjan" is the well-known red bead (coral). It is also said: al-lu'lu' is the large pearls and al-marjan is their small ones. Then the attribution of their coming forth to the two seas, although they only come forth from the salt water, as they have said, is [explained by] what was said: "They only come forth from the meeting place of the salt and the sweet water," or because when the two met and became like one thing, it was permissible to say: "They come forth from the sea," although they do not come forth from the whole sea but from a part of it, and this is the more apparent view. It is also read as "yukhraju" in the passive voice from the causative (ikhraj), and in the active voice with "al-lu'lu' wal-marjan" in the accusative, and with the first-person plural "nun of majesty" (nun al-'azama).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verse 23–24:

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ ﴿And His are the sailing ships (al-jawar)﴾. That is, al-sufun (ships), the plural of jariyah (a sailing vessel). It is also read with a raised ra' and with the yā' omitted, as in the saying of the one who said:

"Her front teeth are four and beautiful, and the four beside them are eight (in all)."

﴿al-munshaʾat (the lofty ones)﴾: those whose sails are raised, or those that are constructed (made). It is also read with a kasra on the shin, meaning: those who raise the sails, or those which bring the waves into being by their running. ﴿In the sea like landmarks﴾: like lofty mountains, the plural of ʿalam, which is a tall mountain.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verse 25–28:

﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾ That is: everyone on the earth among the animals or the moving things. And "man" (من, man) is used for the predominance (of rational beings), or it means "of the two weighty ones" (of humankind and jinn).

﴿Perishing﴾ ceasing to exist, without doubt.

﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ That is: His Essence, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Full of majesty and honour﴾ That is: the One who possesses complete self-sufficiency and perfect bounty. It has also been said: He is the One with whom is majesty and honour for His sincere servants. These are among the greatest of His attributes, exalted is He. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Persist in invoking the Lord of Majesty and Honour" (ألِظُّوا بِياذا الجَلالِ والإكْرامِ, alliẓū bi-yā dhā al-jalāli wa al-ikrām). And from him, upon him be blessings and peace, that he passed by a man who was praying and saying: "O Lord of Majesty and Honour," and he said: "You have been answered." It was also read as "Dhī al-Jalāli wa al-Ikrām" (ذِي الجَلالِ والإكْرامِ) as an attribute of "your Lord." In either case, describing Him, exalted is He, with this after mentioning the perishing and remaining of creation indicates that, exalted is He, after their perishing He still pours upon them the effects of His kindness and generosity, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ That is: His Essence, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verse 29:

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ For their revival into everlasting life and their reward with lasting bliss are the greatest of blessings and the most magnificent of favours.

﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾ all of them, for what they need in their essences and their existences, both in coming into being and in remaining, and all their other states, by a continuous request, whether by the tongue of speech or by the tongue of circumstance. For all of them, in terms of their possible realities, are entirely devoid of any entitlement to existence and to the perfections that branch from it, to such a degree that if the connection between them and the divine care were severed, they would not catch even the scent of existence at all. Thus they are at every moment continually in a state of seeking and asking. This has already been discussed in the interpretation of His exalted words: ﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ in Surah Ibrahim, upon him be peace.

﴿Every day﴾ that is, every moment of time.

﴿He is in a matter﴾ of the matters, among which is the granting of what they asked for. For He, exalted is He, never ceases to bring into being individuals and to enrich others, and to bring about conditions and to remove conditions, as His will requires, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdom. And in the hadith: ﴿Among His matters is that He forgives a sin, relieves a distress, raises a people and abases others.﴾ It has been said: in this is a refutation of the Jews, who say: Allah does not decree anything on the Sabbath day.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verses 30–31:

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ — despite your witnessing of what has been mentioned of His beneficence.

﴿We will attend to you﴾ — i.e., We will devote Ourselves to your reckoning and your recompense, and that is on the Day of Resurrection, when the affairs of creation mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Every day He is in some task﴾ come to an end. Then no affair remains except one, which is the recompense, and so He expressed it as "attending to them" by way of figurative representation. It has also been said that it is borrowed from the saying of one who threatens his companion: "I will attend to you," i.e., I will devote myself to striking you, free from everything that occupies me from it. The intended meaning is concentrating on inflicting harm upon him and taking vengeance on him. It has been read as "sa-yafrughu" (with the verb in the active and in the passive voice), and it has been read as "sa-nafrughu ilaykum," i.e., We will turn towards you.

﴿O you two heavy ones (ath-thaqalan)﴾ — these are mankind and the jinn. They were so named either because of their heaviness upon the earth, or because of the weightiness of their opinions, or because they are burdened with obligation (taklif).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 55, verses 36–37:

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ Indeed, explaining the outcome of what they are upon of disbelief and sins is a kindness (lutf), and what a kindness and what a favour it is.

﴿Then when the sky splits open﴾, i.e., it is cleft asunder on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And it becomes red like rose﴾ like a red rose (wardah). It is also read as "wardatun" with a raised ending, on the basis that kāna is complete (tāmmah), meaning "there came to be a rose-coloured sky," and this falls under the figure of tajrid (abstraction), like the saying of one who said:

The answer to "idha" (when) is omitted, i.e., there will occur, among the states and terrors, what the circle of speech cannot encompass.

﴿فَبِأيِّ: آلاءِ رَبِّكُما تُكَذِّبانِ﴾

Translation of the passage:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿This is Hell, which the criminals deny﴾, is on the assumption of a verb of saying, i.e., it is said to them that by way of rebuke, since the sentence is either a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that comes as an answer to a question arising from the narration of seizing by the forelocks and the feet, as if it were said: "What does He do to them at that time?" ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ ﴿Reclining﴾ is in the accusative (nasb) by way of specification (ikhtisas).

﴿On green cushions (rafraf) of finery﴾. The word rafraf is either a collective noun (ism jins) or a noun of multitude (ism jam'), whose singular is rafrafa. It has been said that it is what hangs down from the beds, from the upper parts of the garments. It has also been said that it is a kind of carpet, or carpets. It has been said that it means cushions, and it has been said that it means cushions of a kind called namariq (fine cushions or rugs). It has also been said that it means any broad garment, and that rafarif are the edges of carpets and the surplus parts of a tent. Rafraf al-sahab is its haydab (the lower fringe of the clouds).

What is meant by it is the category (jins), and for this reason it is described with a plural form, taking the meaning into account, as in "rafraf" according to one of the two views. It is also read as "'ala rafarif khudur" (on green cushions) with two dammas, and as "'abaqiri" like "madaini," a relative form derived from 'abaqir as a place name.

Blessed is the name of your Lord" is a glorification and sanctification (*tanzih* and *taqdis*, declaring Him free of any deficiency) of Him, the Exalted. It affirms what was mentioned in the noble surah of His bounties that overflow upon mankind. That is: exalted is His majestic name, of which is that with which the surah begins, the name *al-Rahman* (the Most Merciful), which indicates His bestowing of the detailed bounties. He is exalted above what is unbefitting of His station, among which is denying His blessings and rejecting them. If the state of His name, merely by its indicating Him, is like this, then what is your thought about His most holy and exalted Essence? It has been said that *al-ism* (the name) here means *al-sifa* (the attribute). It has also been said that it is *muqhham* (superfluous, extraneous), as in the words of the one who said: [Until the year's end, then the name of peace upon you both].
